corrected_answer:
Assumptions: the draft model proposes a fixed number of tokens per step, the target model verifies them with the same decoding policy, and instrumentation can provide synchronized timestamps; hardware, kernels, batching, and workload characteristics must be measured rather than assumed. Scenario variant 258 is not evidence by itself.

Hypothesis: speculative decoding will reduce target-model time per generated token versus target-only decoding only when accepted tokens per verification step offset draft, verification, synchronization, and transfer overhead; for this case it may instead be slower. Pre-register a threshold such as lower median and p95 end-to-end latency per output token with no material correctness change, and treat failure to meet it as falsification.

Measurements: run target-only and speculative modes with identical prompts, sampling parameters, seeds or paired requests, warmup, batch/concurrency, sequence lengths, and output limits. Record draft latency (ms/step and ms/token), target verification latency (ms/step), target-only latency, acceptance rate by position, accepted tokens per step, generated tokens and target evaluations, synchronization/barrier and host-device transfer time, queueing, kernel gaps, memory use, power/thermal state, throughput, median/p95/p99 latency, and cost per output token. Use synchronized tracing with explicit start/stop boundaries so overlapping intervals are not double-counted; verify token accounting and output equivalence under the selected policy.

Controlled experiment: randomize paired requests across target-only and speculative arms, repeat over representative prompt/output-length, batch, concurrency, and workload strata, report medians and confidence intervals, and compare both end-to-end and decomposed latency. Hold model versions, precision, compilation, cache state, placement, scheduler settings, and service limits constant. Separate draft, verification, scheduling, communication, and queueing contributions with trace evidence. Confounders include low acceptance, draft quality, dynamic batching, cache/prefix reuse, contention, clock/thermal throttling, compilation/autotuning, memory pressure, host scheduling, network transfers, and changed stopping or sampling semantics.
